chapter.title: Values
chapter.para: Objects cross between Rexx and Python by reference: a Python list used from Rexx is the list itself, and a Rexx Directory used from Python is the Directory itself. Only the simplest values, strings and numbers, are converted, because each language has its own: a Rexx string is not a Python str, and Python's int, float and str are three different types where Rexx has one.

section.title: Python Values in Rexx
section.para: What a Python call returns, an attribute's value, an item, comes to Rexx as follows:

listitem.para: Python's str, int, float and bytes come back as Rexx strings, with their value. A bool comes back as .Boolean~true or .Boolean~false, which Rexx takes as 1 and 0, its &true; and &false; ().

A float is written as a Rexx number: its shortest digits (those of Python's repr), placed as ooRexx writes x + 0 under numeric digits 17. So it is written plainly unless its integer part needs more than 17 places or its decimals more than 34 (0.0000001, 0.30000000000000004), and otherwise with an uppercase E and a signed exponent (1E+17, 5E-324). A whole number written plainly keeps a .0 (1.0, 10000000000000000.0): it is what makes it a float again when it goes back to Python (the number rule, below). -0.0 is kept. Each of these texts goes back to Python as the same float. NaN and the infinities come as nan, +infinity and -infinity, as ooRexx itself writes them; they are not Rexx numbers, so the number rule sends them back as str; the way back for them is .py~float(x) or .py~box("float", x), which read them as floats.
numpy's scalars (numpy.float64, numpy.int64 and the like) come back as their values, as Rexx strings.
&None; comes back as &nil;.
Everything else comes back as a , by reference: lists, tuples, dicts, sets, numpy arrays, functions, classes, modules, and instances of any class.

example.title: Python values in Rexx
example.programlisting:
say .py~len("abc") .py~abs(-2.5) .py~bool(1) .py~eval("b'bytes'") say (.py~eval("None") == .nil) np = .py~import("numpy") x = np~float64(2.5) say x x~class~id -- a numpy scalar: a Rexx string l = .py~eval("[1, 2]") say l l~class~id -- a list: a PyObject
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Rexx Values in Python
section.para: The arguments of a call to Python, a value assigned to an attribute or an item, go to Python as follows:

listitem.para: A Rexx string goes as:
an int when it is a whole number written canonically: 0, 42, -7, with no leading zeros, blanks or plus sign;

a float when it is any other Rexx number with a decimal point or an exponent: 3.14, 1E3. Like any float, it is rounded to the nearest double: 3.14159265358979323846264 is 3.141592653589793 (.py~decimal(x) keeps every digit). -0.0 is the float -0.0, and -0, a whole number, the int 0;

a decimal.Decimal, exact, when the float would be a value of another kind: when the number overflows (1E999, -1E999 would be infinite) or underflows (1E-999 would be zero, and it is not zero). It comes back to Rexx as a PyObject, as .py~decimal gives;
a str otherwise: "007", " 5", "+5", and any text.
&nil; goes as &None;.
A Boolean goes as a bool ().

A Rexx Array goes as a Python list, a copy, its items converted by the same rules (nested Arrays as nested lists). An empty slot goes as &None;, so the list has the Array's size. A multi-dimensional Array goes as lists nested by dimension, the first outermost: a 2×3 Array m is a list of 2 lists of 3, where m[i, j] is Python's m[i-1][j-1], which numpy takes as a 2-D array. The copy has the structure of the original: an Array that contains itself is a list that contains itself, Arrays that contain each other keep the cycle, and an Array that appears twice in one value is one list. Arrays nested more than 1000 deep cannot be copied (a ValueError).
A PyObject goes as its Python object.
Any other Rexx object goes by reference, as an , and comes back to Rexx as the object itself.

section.para: This is the number rule. It looks only at the value, never at the function that receives it, so that it can be applied by reading the program. Python never turns a string into a number by itself, so numbers must go as numbers: math~sqrt(2), random~randint(1, 6), row[0] and numpy depend on it. Its one pitfall is text that looks like a number, such as the file name "2026"; see .

example.title: Rexx values in Python
example.programlisting:
kind = .py~eval("lambda x: type(x).__name__") -- the type's name say kind~new(42) kind~new(-7) kind~new(3.14) kind~new(1E3) say kind~new("007") kind~new(" 5") kind~new("+5") kind~new("abc") say kind~new((1, 2)) kind~new(.nil) kind~new(.directory~new)
::requires "python.cls"
example.screen: int int float float str str str str list NoneType RexxObject

example.title: A Rexx object goes to Python and comes back as itself
example.programlisting:
d = .directory~new l = .py~list((d,)) -- a Python list holding the Directory say (l[0] == d) l[0]~class~id
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Booleans
section.para: Rexx's &true; and &false; are the strings 1 and 0: nothing tells &false; from the number 0. For a real boolean, python.cls brings the Boolean class, from boolean.cls, which the ooRexx bridges share and which is proposed for ooRexx itself. It has two instances, .Boolean~true and .Boolean~false, that are 1 and 0 wherever Rexx uses them (IF, operators, DATATYPE, string methods) and answer isA(.Boolean); .Boolean~of(value) gives the one for a logical value.

listitem.para: Python's True and False come to Rexx as .Boolean~true and .Boolean~false.
A Boolean goes to Python as True or False, so a bool that goes through Rexx and back is still a bool.
&true; and &false; go as the ints 1 and 0, by the number rule, except to a parameter annotated bool (below).

example.title: Booleans
example.programlisting:
t = .py~eval("1 < 2") say t t~class~id (t + 1) json = .py~import("json") say json~dumps(.array~of(.Boolean~true, .true))
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Parameters Annotated bool
section.para: Rexx's &true; and &false; are the strings 1 and 0, so by the number rule they go to Python as ints. One exception is taken from the called function's own annotations: a 1 or 0 passed to a parameter annotated bool goes as True or False, so that &true; works for pandas' inplace=. For a function without annotations that insists on a real bool, pass .Boolean~true (or .py~box("bool", 1)).

example.title: 1 and 0 to a parameter annotated bool
example.programlisting:
.py~exec("def flag(on: bool): return repr(on)") flag = .py~main~getattr("flag") say flag~new(1) flag~new(.false) flag~new(2) plain = .py~eval("lambda on: repr(on)") say plain~new(1)
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Choosing the Python Type
section.para: When the number rule picks the wrong type, the type can be given:

listitem.para:
, , and
make the Python str, int, float or decimal.Decimal and keep it as a PyObject, so that it is not converted back into a Rexx string. decimal keeps all of Rexx's digits.
makes an object of any type from the text of a value, never through the number rule.

example.title: Choosing the type
example.programlisting:
kind = .py~eval("lambda x: type(x).__name__") say kind~new(.py~str(2026)) kind~new(.py~int("12")) kind~new(.py~float(1)) say .py~decimal("1") / .py~decimal("3") say .py~box("bytes", "ab") .py~box("fraction", "3/4") .py~box("bool", 1)
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Modules that Want Strings
section.para: For a module that works mostly with text that may look like a number (file names, identifiers, codes), .py~import(name, "string") sends every Rexx string as a str, whatever it looks like. It applies to the calls made through that module and through everything reached from it: its attributes (os~path), what its calls return, and their items. Positions and keys in o[k] keep the number rule, so that l[0] works on a list it returned; the bool exception stays. "number", the default, is the number rule.

The mark changes what the module receives, not what it returns: a module imported as "string" that needs a number gets the text (json~dumps(x, .py~kw("indent", 0)) would get the text "0"), and must be given one with int or box.

example.title: A module imported as "string"
example.programlisting:
os = .py~import("posixpath", "string") say os~join("archive", "2026") plain = .py~import("posixpath") signal on syntax say plain~join("archive", "2026") -- 2026 goes as an int exit syntax: say condition("O")~message
::requires "python.cls"
example.screen: archive/2026 Python error: TypeError: join() argument must be str, bytes, or os.PathLike object, not 'int'.

section.title: Rexx Values in Python Programs

indexterm.secondary: results of Rexx code in Python

section.para: The number rule applies the other way too, to what Rexx returns to Python (the results of eval, of a routine, of a message to a Rexx object) and to the arguments Rexx passes when Python calls it back: a Rexx string that is a number by the rule comes as an int or a float, any other as a str; &nil; as &None;; an Array as a list (a copy); a PyObject as its Python object; and any other Rexx object as an oorexx.RexxObject, by reference. A Python object that goes to Rexx and back is the object itself.

example.title: Rexx values in Python
example.programlisting:
import oorexx
with oorexx.Interpreter() as rexx: for e in ['42', '"007"', '3.14', '.nil', '.array~of(1, "a")', '.directory~new']: v = rexx.eval(e) print(e, '->', type(v).__name__, repr(v)) same = rexx.routine("return arg(1)") d = {} print(same(d) is d)
example.screen: 42 -> int 42 "007" -> str '007' 3.14 -> float 3.14 .nil -> NoneType None .array~of(1, "a") -> list [1, 'a'] .directory~new -> RexxObject <Rexx a Directory> True
